name: Failures, Fires, and Recalls
scope: Shipped disasters and their mechanisms; the one-cent coin-cell cost-down that bricked the product

claims.claim_text: The dangerous class of counterfeit power semiconductor is not the empty package but the underspecified one: parts sold as capable of dissipating around 50 W contained genuine dies rated for about 5 W, so assemblies passed test, worked for a week and then failed once in service.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were actually genuine silicon in there, but they were undersized
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The true cost of a counterfeit component is the field service call it eventually causes, not the price of the part and its assembly, which is why gray-market sourcing is avoided even on low-volume products where unit cost is not the binding constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost isn't just the cost of that part and fitting it. It's cost of going out to the field and actually repairing it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A counterfeit transistor with no die at all inside a TO-220 package presents as an open circuit or a fire risk rather than as a degraded part, which is a different and more abrupt failure mode than an undersized die.
claims.quote_verbatim: You just have a TO220 package and you might have, you might have a little fire on your hands

claims.claim_text: Reworking a solder joint purely because it looks cosmetically poor usually reduces its long-term reliability rather than improving it, because the additional thermal cycle grows the intermetallic layer; appearance is not on its own a reason to touch a working joint.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go back to retouch a joint because it looks ugly or something, they said the majority of the time, you're going to end up degrading
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: Silicon defects that survive production test are usually narrow boundary conditions, and the way to get them acknowledged is to capture the exact bus transaction with a logic analyser and hand the vendor's test engineers a reproducible address boundary and timing; in one case this exposed a defect in the part's address decoder.
claims.quote_verbatim: we sent the part back and we told the test engineers, it's this exact, like if you hit it with this exact address boundary, with this exact timing
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Automotive customers work to a zero parts-per-million target, which in practice means any field failure is returned to the supplier and the supplier is expected to establish root cause and put a corrective action in place rather than to treat it as within tolerance.
claims.quote_verbatim: in automotive, they're generally like you're at, you're generally striving for zero PPM
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: The most common cause of microcontrollers bricking themselves in the field after months of service is inadequate brownout protection: a large holding capacitor keeps the rail at around 1.2 to 1.5 volts, well below the minimum operating voltage but high enough for the part to keep executing code, and when power returns the device does not reliably reset before writing to flash or EEPROM and corrupts it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's sitting at some voltage like a volt and a half or 1.2 volts. You know, it's well below the VDD min, but it's allowed to execute code
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Corrupted flash or EEPROM reported as a silicon defect is very often a system design problem instead, and it is fully preventable with a proper brownout or supervisor circuit; failures of this kind are described as frequent flyers in returns analysis but are not defects in the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: almost every one of those things that I've looked at has been a situation with an improper brownout circuit
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Solenoid drive is a firmware safety problem as much as a hardware one: a coil energised and not turned off within its rated duty will overheat, smoke and can catch fire, so the timing that limits on-time is a safety function, not a feature.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you hit a solenoid, you've got to turn it on, but you have to turn it off in a very, if you don't turn it off, it'll smoke and possibly catch fire
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Electromechanical game driver boards were built around arrays of Darlington transistors in the TIP102 class, rated 60 to 100 V and five to fifteen amps, fed from a four-bit latched data bus with separate latch assertion lines, with roughly a quarter of the outputs driving high-current solenoids and the rest incandescent lamps.
claims.quote_verbatim: they typically have like the equivalent, their, their older parts are like 6305s, but their, their equivalent to like tip 102s
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: A convenient-looking metal surface such as a fat heatsink inside a UPS may sit at 400 volts DC with no fuse in the path, so the ground reference for a scope probe must be established from the schematic rather than assumed from what looks like chassis metal.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's 400 volts DC with no fuse
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: A DC arc has no current zero crossing to extinguish it, so a fault in a high-voltage DC isolator sustains the arc until something burns; this is why rooftop solar DC isolators at around 460 volts have been a recurring fire source and why microinverter architectures, which keep the array wiring at low voltage and combine at AC, are inherently safer.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you've got high voltage, high power DC, if that sucker arcs over, there it is. It just keeps going. It's a DC. That arc sustains until something catches on fire
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Multiple brands of solar DC isolator have been subject to safety recalls after field failures, which makes the isolator, rather than the panels or the inverter, a component worth checking on an installed array.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's been recalls of various brands have had to be recalled because they're not safe
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A recall of failing touchscreen units in 135,000 Tesla cars was defended on the grounds that the units had only ever been expected to last five to six years, which in a vehicle where the touchscreen carries essentially all controls makes the design life of a single subsystem the design life of the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: Tesla has responded to a United States recall of failing touchscreens in 135,000 of its cars, arguing the units were only ever expected to last five years
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The Takata airbag inflator recall covered roughly 67 million units, with about 17 deaths and 200 injuries attributed to inflators firing incorrectly, and 130,000 cars recalled in Australia alone, from a single component supplier of about 50,000 employees.
claims.quote_verbatim: 17 people have died, apparently, from these. And 200 injuries from these airbags
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A component as trivial as a rubber band caused a recall costing on the order of 20 million dollars, which is the standard illustration that recall cost is set by the accessibility of the fault rather than by the value of the part at fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's due to a rubber band
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Repairing a fault sealed inside a hundred-metre marine seismic streamer required developing a surgical procedure from scratch: cutting the outer sheath open with a scalpel, then building purpose-made tools to grip and retract the sheath because it could not be pulled back by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to develop techniques to actually repair these, which involved actually getting a scalpel, cutting open, like it's, it's like surgery
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Medical device regulatory testing requires the system to keep functioning through applied EMI, ESD and magnetic field disturbance rather than merely to survive them, so a reset or a crash on an ESD pulse is a failure of the test, not an acceptable recovery.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got applied EMI issues, applied ESD issues, magnetic field issues, and things like that where the system has to keep working throughout all of that stuff
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: A recurring pattern in devices that fail regulatory EMC testing is a digital-led design with no ESD protection and single-ended, ground-referenced data leaving the board on cables, with no error detection and no common-mode rejection; each of those omissions is individually survivable on a bench and collectively fatal in a hostile environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was ground reference signal going off of a board, which is a suicide jump when you're trying to have something work in a hostile environment
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Treating a marked component value as the actual value is a common source of unexplained behaviour: a nominal 0.1 microfarad capacitor's real capacitance depends heavily on the dielectric and the applied conditions, and academic training rarely covers the non-ideal behaviour of basic passives.
claims.quote_verbatim: The reality is something very different depending upon what the actual capacitor is
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Whether a product must be battery powered is an architectural decision worth challenging explicitly, because removing the battery removes a whole class of reliability and service failures; wireless and battery operation are frequently product expectations rather than requirements.
claims.quote_verbatim: I prefer things that plug into the wall just for reliability, get the batteries out of the equation
claims.speaker: Jerry Twomey
claims.episode_title: Applied Embedded Electronics with Jerry Twomey

claims.claim_text: Power should never be carried through a single via, because the resistance of an individual via is not well controlled and a via can crack under mechanical or thermal stress; multiple vias in parallel provide both lower resistance and redundancy against one of them failing.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're using just one via to pass power through, you're doing it wrong
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: Solder-filling power vias serves reliability as well as resistance: it reduces the current density in the plating and removes the barrel as a single mechanical failure point. Via resistance is essentially irrelevant on signal traces, so this applies only to power nets.
claims.quote_verbatim: which is part of the reason why you also solder fill these vias as well because it's for reliability for power nets as well as decreasing the resistance
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: Power vias should be left untented if the board will see a wave solder process, because the wave will then fill them, giving lower resistance and better reliability at no additional cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you always leave your vias, your power vias untented so that if you do have a wave solder process, you can actually get the benefit of having the wave bubble up and fill your vias
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: Reliability effort is a function of who bears the consequences: a commodity consumer product built to a monthly schedule prices warranty returns in and ships whatever the design state is at the deadline, whereas an industrial or test-and-measurement product takes eighteen months and slips further, because the manufacturer's reputation rather than the unit is what is at risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: People producing these tablets, right? They don't have a reputation to protect
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: In a modular product the connection points are where reliability is won or lost, and this remains true when there is no discrete connector and only mating contact surfaces; the mechanical quality of the interface has to be designed deliberately.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you want to design and reliability into that, you need good connection points
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: A confidently argued warranty claim that the design is at fault frequently turns out to be an assembly error by the claimant, in one case a five-volt regulator fitted backwards, which is an argument for checking supply rails methodically before accepting a design fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: you find that they've soldered the 5-volt regulator in backwards
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Products with substantial mechanical content carry warranty return rates that swamp their electronics: for a 3D printer class machine, replacement of something like one unit in twenty to thirty would not be surprising, which has to be priced in before the product ships.
claims.quote_verbatim: you may replace that. I wouldn't be surprised if someone was replacing one out of every 20 or one out of every 30
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: When a low-volume product uses a part whose field reliability is genuinely unknown, offering an unconditional free replacement is a deliberate way to buy failure data: the exposure is bounded by the small unit count, and the returns tell the designer which part to change in the next revision.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to add like, you know, an infinite warranty on that part. If it dies, I'll replace it, um, immediately and for free
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Professional liability cover for an independent embedded design consultant is genuinely hard to obtain: a four-month search through local agents, online providers and a professional body's insurance partner produced quotes only through Lloyd's of London, at a premium described as astronomically high.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I took me about four months actually
claims.speaker: Jeremiah Gillis

claims.claim_text: The reason embedded consultants struggle to buy professional liability cover is structural rather than about risk level: insurers price from actuarial tables, and there is no table for embedded design work, so the more precisely the work is described the further outside a priced category the applicant falls.
claims.quote_verbatim: insurance companies work off actuarial tables. And if they can't like put you on a table

claims.claim_text: Force majeure clauses present in most supply contracts release a supplier from the contracted delivery date, and during supply disruption they are invoked broadly enough that the contracted date stops being a planning input at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the, uh, suppliers are like shouting force majeure, which is a thing that's in many, many contracts. It basically means that you don't, don't have to deliver on the date
claims.speaker: Kieran O'Leary

claims.claim_text: Pricing a work warranty into a consulting engagement up front means small post-delivery changes can be absorbed without a fresh negotiation at the moment the client is least willing to pay, and functions as a credible quality signal rather than as pure cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can kind of build in the warranty, the work warranty into your price upfront
claims.speaker: Alex Klimai

claims.claim_text: For a reseller of moderate-value instruments, the administrative cost of claiming an individual unit against the factory warranty exceeded the value of the claim, so failures were absorbed instead; the calculation only flips once the failure rate rises far enough that returns accumulate into a batch.
claims.quote_verbatim: Do I bother even claiming that under warranty from Bryman or from Kane? Test? No, I don't bother. I just eat the cost
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A manufacturing defect in the OLED module used in a family of Agilent and Keysight handheld meters caused a high enough failure rate, with the original display no longer purchasable, that a third party reverse-engineered the display protocol and built an STM32-based translator board to drive a currently available OLED in its place.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got some manufacturing defect that fails in all these meters
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A 2020 model electric vehicle was recalled worldwide for a fault that could short the traction battery and cause a fire, and the remedy delivered was a software update to the battery management behaviour rather than replacement of the cells.
claims.quote_verbatim: could just spontaneously short out the battery and explode, which is not optimal
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A silicon vendor redesigned the LMH6518 variable-gain amplifier used in the front end of most modern oscilloscopes and reduced its tolerance of the 400 millivolt input offset the original part supported, without changing the part number and with the change buried in the datasheet; there are documented cases of instruments being bricked by front-end DC offset as a result.
claims.quote_verbatim: they changed the design of that chip as well. Without sort of, you know, if you have to read deep in the data sheet, they didn't change the part number
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Dual-sourcing a chip across two foundries has largely been abandoned for digital parts because it is too costly and the processes are not compatible enough to port between, so supply continuity now rests on the fact that a large foundry operates several fabs able to run the same process.
claims.quote_verbatim: if there's an earthquake or a fire in one place, you may still be able to at least manufacture a percentage of what you had
claims.speaker: Oyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

attribution_notes: ep532: speaker_repaired alternates between Dave Jones and Chris Gammell across the +/-1 paragraph windows and is frequently offset by one turn. The claims taken from this episode (DC arc sustain and solar isolator fires, the Takata figures, the Tesla touchscreen recall, the seismic streamer repair procedure) are Dave Jones's own accounts and reading, and are attributed to him on content grounds.

ep492 passage 61: the actuarial-table explanation is voiced by the host summarising, not by the consultant whose story it is, so speaker is null.
